summary:
Quintana Roo stands under the national framework of Mexico, where extending legal gender recognition to trans people remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure by that date, while six states (Aguascalientes, Chiapas, Durango, Querétaro, Tabasco and Tamaulipas) had reformed nothing, leaving trans residents carrying documents permanently mismatched to their lived identity.

The same Human Rights Watch feature documents coercive detention and border scrutiny as risks for travellers whose documents contradict their presentation, hazards that fall hardest where recognition procedures are absent or obstructed. Quintana Roo enacted legal gender recognition in 2020, so a trans visitor's papers are not automatically a point of friction at the state level, although national reporting indicates that formal recognition does not guarantee consistent treatment.

Partnership and family rights are settled in Quintana Roo. Same-sex marriage has been permitted in the state since 2012: two marriages performed in Kantunilkín in November 2011 were annulled by the governor in April 2012 and reinstated on 3 May 2012 once the state conceded that its Civil Code sets no gender requirement. The Quintana Roo congress legalized adoption by same-sex couples in August 2022. Nationally, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009.

The state penal code punishes crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender as hate crimes, and Quintana Roo ratified the 2011 federal constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination.

Quintana Roo banned conversion practices on 15 December 2023, following the example set by Morelos. Both legislatures approved initiatives prohibiting and sanctioning 'Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género' (ECOSIG), commonly called conversion therapies. Penalties run to two to six years in prison and fines of 1,000 to 2,000 times the daily UMA value for those who carry out such practices, and the reform applies across the state, including the tourist corridors of Cancún and the Riviera Maya.

Violence against trans people nationally gives the legal picture its context. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to the 100 recorded in another country in the region. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.
